newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Migraine no headache for drugs companies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Migraine no headache for drugs companies.

text.p: AMSTERDAM, June 25, Reuter - Charles Darwin had them. So did Thomas Jefferson, Sigmund Freud and Leo Tolstoy.

They had to suffer their migraine attacks with little more than a vinegar-soaked cloth across the brow to ease the blinding headaches, nausea, and sensitivity to light that makes normal life impossible for hours and even days on end.
Now, drugs companies are racing to find the best treatment for migraine, which affects 585 million people -- one in 10 of the world's population.
With migraine the developed world's most common neurological disease, whoever can find a safe and effective drug is assured of huge profits.
The market for prescription migraine drugs is dominated by Britain's Glaxo Wellcome but up to eight rival drugs are in development or have just gone on sale.
"There will be a serious battle in the market because the products are pretty comparable," said James Culverwell, a pharmaceuticals analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
Glaxo Wellcome's drug sumatriptan, marketed as Imitrex in the United States and Imigran in Europe, is estimated to hold more than 70 percent of a worldwide market worth $1.1 billion.
It also owns naratriptan, a longer-acting migraine medicine which has just gone on sale as Naramig.

Companies promoting rival products at the 8th Congress of the International Headache Society in Amsterdam earlier this month included Merck and Co with rizatriptan, marketed as MAXALT, Zeneca Group with zolmitriptan (Zomig) and Pfizer with eletriptan.
Vanguard Medical is testing a migraine remedy in conjunction with Smithkline Beecham.
At an estimated $400 million to bring a drug to market, companies must be sure of trends in their markets.
"We believe the market will grow considerably over the next few years. It's an under-satisfied market from a business perspective," said Chris Dalton of Zeneca Pharmaceuticals.

He said between 19 and 60 percent of migraine sufferers did not consult doctors after an attack, instead using cheaper over-the-counter analgesics such as aspirin. The percentage varies widely according to country and age.
COUNTING THE ECONOMIC COST OF MIGRAINE
He said doctors were already realising the economic cost of migraine, with 18 million working days affected every year.
The cost to the U.S. economy alone in terms of lost productivity has been estimated at between $5.6 billion and $17.2 billion a year.
Dalton said the market for prescription migraine drugs could more than double to $2.45 billion by 2000.
Little wonder the posters detailing alternative treatments such as peppermint oil, acupuncture, hypnotherapy and light therapy, were tucked away into a remote corner of the conference centre.

Most of the recent research has focused on 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), better known as serotonin. This key neurotransmitter -- which carries chemical messages betwen cells -- is known to be involved in migraine although scientists are not sure how.
After two decades of research, Wellcome launched sumatriptan in 1991 to target 5-HT receptors -- doorways that allow the 5-HT molecules to lock onto and act upon cells.
Sumatriptan helps control the dilation of blood vessels that occurs during attacks.
"It was probably the most significant advance in the treatment of migraine this century," said U.S. neurologist Fred Sheftell of the New England Centre for Headache.
Now the 5-HT receptors are divided into a dozen different subtypes, all of which can be tackled in different ways. The more specific the action of a drug, the fewer side-effects there will be.
Before, the most effective specific treatments were ergotamines, drugs based on naturally occurring fungi, but which can cause side-effects including vomiting and can themselves induce headache.
Sheftell said the success of sumatriptan, coinciding with an expansion in scientific understanding of the disease, exposed the scope of the worldwide market.
HIGH PRICE BARRIER TO NEW PRODUCTS
He said the new products were all potentially effective and increased the range of choice for doctors and patients, but their high price was a barrier.
Sumatriptan sells for about 4.95 pounds ($8.00) per tablet in Britain.
"It's going to be a question of which company will be the first to break that barrier," he said.

Peter Goatsby, clinical neurologist at London's National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, said knowledge of migraine had increased dramatically in the last decade as research focused on the genetic causes, imaging of the brain during attacks and drug treatments.
He said pharmaceutical companies were recognising the potential size of the market as sumatriptan was being used by only about 10 percent of migraine sufferers.
"What the other companies see is the 90 percent," he said.
He said it was too early to say which drug would emerge as the industry standard, adding that each one could be suitable for different people.
Culverwell said sumatriptan had not achieved a greater penetration of the market by reaching more sufferers, which indicated potential sales were not as large as some thought.
But he said price discounting, the increased range of products and more intensive marketing would expand the size of the market. It could double over the next five years, he said.
He also said Glaxo-Wellcome was bound to lose market share as rival drugs went on sale.
But the British giant is not yielding to the competition, instead vowing to continue its development of migraine drugs.
"We are committed to sustaining leadership in this area," said Lucy Williams, Glaxo-Wellcome's product communications manager.
She did not expect any slowing of sales of sumatriptan, which may be launched as a nasal spray in the United States and other markets.
Williams said the overall market could grow because migraine was so common. But she added that doctors still rarely prescribed drugs for it.
